items.title: Arthur "Monk" Hazel Interview, 1959-07-16
items.q: it was like Fazola playing the saxophone. Fazola was the world's worst sounding saxophone player that you ever heard in your life.

ctx.x: Was it good or is it funny?

It was marvelous Bill, but it was the stinkinest tone, it was like Fazola playing the saxophone. Fazola was the world's worst sounding saxophone player that you ever heard in your life. In fact, cause Benny Pollock, two or three times, well not only Pollock, but Miller. And a lot of the band wanted him to play the lead, cause Fazola was a marvelous musician, you know. I mean he read the seven clefs and all. But man, the tone he got out of the saxophone, the sound of Sidney Ironman, the same Rapolo was the same…
But what about Snoozer? You were going to tell about how?

items.title: Arthur "Monk" Hazel Interview, 1967-10-28
items.q: And, uh, I got Fazola for him.

ctx.x: What was Glenn Miller's, uh, what was Glenn Miller's, uh, aspiration at that time? Did he want to continue to be a jazz trombone player? Did he want to write even in those days?

He liked to, he liked to write more than anything. I'm going to tell you something that maybe you might not know. But Glenn Miller has built more bands, more jazz bands, than any man in the country. The first band he built was Ben Pollack's band, in which Benny Goodman was at the time, Jimmy Mac Paul and all those kind of guys. The next band he built was, uh, was Ray Noble's band when he came over here from England, which was the best band in the country at the time. Uh, he built the Claude Thornhill's, I think,…
